messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar Haddad is a 41-year-old single man who works the evening shift at a fast-food restaurant, usually on the grill and fryer where the kitchen is full of sharp commands, timers, and sudden clatter. He came to treatment after months of telling himself he could manage if he just kept his world small enough. By the time he asked for help, he was spending most of his life moving between a few places he regarded as tolerable—his apartment, his sister’s living room, and the back kitchen at work when the pace was predictable—and feeling exposed almost everywhere else.

The event he returns to happened late in the day, just as daylight was starting to drain out of the sky. He had been standing outside a neighborhood store when an argument broke out nearby. What stays with him is not a broad summary but the exact sequence: voices rising, a harsh correction shouted by one man at another, then the abrupt crack of violence and the chaos that followed. Omar was not physically injured, but he witnessed another person being attacked at close range. He remembers the helplessness of standing there as the scene became suddenly dangerous, the shock of loud sounds around him, people yelling over one another, and the awful sense that everything changed in a second. The hour itself feels stamped into him. As evening approaches now, he feels his body tighten before he has fully registered why.

In the months afterward, he found that certain moments pulled him back into the same state of alarm. Loud noises were the clearest. In the restaurant, a metal tray dropped on the tile floor or a coworker slamming the freezer door could make him jolt and scan the room before he had consciously thought about where he was. He began listening for noise before it happened, keeping part of his attention trained on the sounds around him. Unexpected sound felt especially dangerous to him; he was certain that if something loud happened without warning, it could mean that something terrible was already underway. His coworkers noticed that he would go rigid when the kitchen erupted or when customers shouted across the counter.

Being corrected had also become charged in a way that embarrassed him. If a manager said, “No, do it this way,” or snapped at him during the dinner rush, Omar felt a surge of fear and humiliation that seemed larger than the moment. It was not ordinary dislike of criticism. In his mind, harsh correction had become linked with the instant before the violence he witnessed, as though raised voices and being told sharply that he was wrong signaled that a situation could turn dangerous without warning. He tried to hide his reaction, but at times he would go quiet for the rest of the shift or ask to work in the back where there was less direct contact.

The same time of day remained especially difficult. As late afternoon moved toward evening, Omar often felt himself bracing. If he was scheduled for that part of the shift, he watched the clock. The changing light, the usual rush building at work, and the sense of the day narrowing toward that hour made him feel exposed. He did not describe this as a memory coming back in words; it was more that the time itself carried threat. He would leave tasks half-finished to check outside the back door or ask coworkers what was taking so long if a delivery or employee was late.

Delays had become another source of alarm. If someone said they would arrive in ten minutes and they were not there, Omar’s mind went quickly to catastrophe. If his sister did not answer her phone right away, if the bus was delayed, if the manager stayed too long in the office after calling someone in to talk, he assumed something bad was happening. Waiting had become intolerable because uncertainty no longer felt neutral to him. He described himself as unable to relax unless things happened exactly when expected.

Over time, he narrowed his life around places he considered safe. He went to work and home and occasionally to his sister’s apartment, but little else. He turned down invitations, avoided unfamiliar stores, and tried not to be out in the evening unless necessary. Even at work, a place he still managed to attend, he felt safest in very specific spots: near the prep counter, with familiar coworkers, when he knew who was in the kitchen and what sounds to expect. The consequence was that his world had become small and fragile. Any change in routine—a new supervisor, a delayed shipment, a burst of shouting from the dining area—could unsettle him for hours.

What finally brought Omar to treatment was a recent incident at work when a supervisor corrected him sharply during the dinner rush and, almost at the same moment, a stack of pans crashed to the floor behind him. He froze, then had to step outside because he was sure something awful was about to happen. Standing in the alley behind the restaurant in the fading light, he realized how few places still felt safe and how much of each day he spent waiting for danger. He says he wants help because he is tired of living as if the worst can start at any moment, and what frightens him most is the idea that his life will keep shrinking until there is nowhere left he can go without feeling on guard.
